CodexText: Red corundum. The same mineral as sapphire, coloured red by traces of chromium. Mozambique is now the most productive source; Myanmar supplied most of the market historically.
SourceRefs: TODO depths; GIA ruby research; Ganoksin production update

CodexText: Blue corundum, coloured by iron and titanium. Sri Lankan gravels, Madagascar and Myanmar are the working sources; Kashmir material is essentially old stock.
SourceRefs: TODO depths; Lotus Gemology sapphire market update 2020; JCK

CodexText: Corundum in the pink range. The Ratnapura gravels yield blues, yellows, pinks, greens and purples from the same wash, which is why one site can teach the whole rarity ladder.
Any corundum that is neither red nor blue. Sold as fancy sapphire, and common in Sri Lankan and Madagascan parcels.
Green beryl, coloured by chromium or vanadium. Zambia is a major modern source, and laboratories can separate origins by trace-element chemistry.
SourceRefs: TODO depths; Ganoksin production update; GIA Gems & Gemology Winter 2019

CodexText: Blue beryl from pegmatites. Minas Gerais is the most-represented locality in the Smithsonian Geogallery spotlight, and home of the Dom Pedro aquamarine.
Purple quartz, grown in gas cavities in basalt flows. One of the most common items in museum reference sets, and a good early-game find.
Banded chalcedony formed as silica gels line a cavity in lava. The bands record each pulse of mineral-bearing water.
Chalcedony with thin iron-oxide layers that interfere with light, giving a flame-like play of colour. Found in volcanic nodules.
